Anderson is the Electric City — a textile-era county seat in the upstate foothills, standing a few miles from Lake Hartwell's shore, with a historic downtown, mill-village streets, and neighbourhoods of early-1900s homes under mature canopy. Its wildlife work is the old-industrial pattern with a lake at its shoulder: bats in the tall attics of the historic homes, raccoons in the chimneys, gray squirrels through the canopy streets, rats in the older commercial and mill roofs — and at the city's west edge, the lake and the Seneca River bottoms pressing beaver and raccoon work into the low properties.

The mill heritage built a particular housing stock: rows of mill cottages with low rooflines and shared canopy, where a squirrel pattern is a street pattern. Our Anderson inspections read the mill streets as systems — the same cottage detail failing the same way house after house — and the historic districts as individual buildings, because each of those was built once, by hand, and hides its entries accordingly.
Anderson.extendedBody:
Mill villages, historic districts, and two kinds of read

Anderson's mill cottages concentrate risk in a handful of details repeated by the row: the eave returns, the unscreened gable vents, the porch junctions. Sealing in metal at those details ends the pattern at your house, and naming the detail — which we do in writing — lets the street learn its own roofs. The historic homes take the opposite approach: a complete individual mapping of layered rooflines, brick chimneys, and a century of junctions, with bat colonies in the tall attics excluded on SCDNR's timing guidance — never sealed in while pups are flightless, every gap closed when the season allows.

The state's rules, in Anderson

South Carolina does not license wildlife operators; SCDNR maintains a referral list, and claims of a state license are invented. Removal in Anderson runs on the depredation permit for your property under §50-11-2570(A) — free, species-specific, thirty days, a year for beaver — carrying the handling rules: rabies-suspect animals reported through SC DPH, bats on the guidance calendar. On the lake side, beaver work in the Seneca bottoms and the Hartwell feeder creeks is the standing ground item, and the year-long permit is what makes honest reach management possible there.

The lake shoulder

West-side Anderson properties add the waterfront read — docks, boathouses, and the creek bottoms — to the building inspection, because Hartwell's shoreline population commutes exactly the way every lake population does: water to structure to roof, nightly.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Honea Path home?
faqs.a: Bat work here is exclusion only, and no permit is required to remove bats in South Carolina. What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.

Pelzer.extendedBody:
The row, the river, and the mill roofs

Pelzer's housing was built by the mill, to the mill's plans, and its wildlife risk lives in the repetition: eave details, gable vents, and porch junctions identical from one end of a street to the other. Squirrels hold the canopy over the rows and commute them; raccoons take the chimneys. Above the cottages, the old mill structures themselves carry their own tenancy — bats in the tall industrial voids, pigeons and rats in the roof systems — building-scale work that ends with sealing, not devices. Down the bluff, the Saluda bottoms run the wet work: beaver dams in the side branches, managed on the year-long depredation permit §50-11-2570(A) provides for the species.

Authorization, South Carolina style

There is no SCDNR operator license — the agency's referral list is a listing, not a credential — and in a town Pelzer's size that is easy to verify and worth verifying. Our work runs on the depredation permit for your property, with the state's handling rules: bats excluded on SCDNR's timing guidance, never sealed in while pups are flightless; rabies-suspect animals reported through SC DPH. The permit is free, species-specific, and arranged as part of the job; the explanation of it, before the quote, is the credential that exists in this state.

The bluff and the bottoms

Pelzer's lots step down toward the river, and the stepped ground hides the usual doors: downhill crawlspaces tall and unscreened, uphill soffits a step from the bank. The full read — attic, crawlspace, every level of the roof — is the Pelzer standard, because the entry nobody inspected is the one the street's squirrels are already using.
